units.unit: Needs a definition of subdivided units and their conditions first
Then evidence about what rent control did in Hong Kong
Claim would be about whether tightening rent control helps tenants
D1 gives the definition and basic conditions
D2 gives actual rent and stock numbers
D11 is tenant survey data showing what tenants want
Tenants pay a 15-25 percent premium per square foot
The 2021 ordinance only capped increases, not the starting rent
Stock still grew after the ordinance, so moderate regulation did not push landlords out
Rent burden still worsened from 31 to 34 percent
The current cap is too weak
Tenants care more about security of tenure and a faster public housing offer than rent level
Wants a source arguing the other side about supply when rent control is tightened
It needs to show tighter rent control reduces supply or quality in marginal housing like SDUs
Ideally with theory plus evidence from another city
Wants a comparative case
To check if a tighter cap changes burden, needs evidence on what happened when a stricter cap was tried somewhere
D6 gives the economic theory on supply
D7 is a real case of a strict cap and what happened after
D5 is the landlords' side to judge how much to trust it
Hard caps on starting rent shrink supply (elasticity 0.31 to 0.48)
Caps on increases like Hong Kong's 2021 one have small or null effects
That fits the stable stock in D2
A hard cap would probably hurt the very tenants it is meant to help
Berlin shows insiders gain and outsiders pay
D5 predicts landlords will exit
D5 admits it has no real margin data and a weak 34 percent response survey
Trusts D5 less than D6 and D7
Now leans against a hard initial-rent cap but for strengthening the increase cap and tenure security
Picks option 1, claim, evidence, objection, reply
Because the main move is arguing against a hard cap while answering the tenant burden point
Hong Kong should keep and strengthen the cap on rent increases and add tenure security
Should not impose a hard cap on initial rent because first-generation caps shrink stock
The cost falls on outsiders
Tenants themselves rank tenure security above rent level
D11p3 backs a narrow tightening: tenure security plus a light band on initial rents, not a hard cap
A light band is acceptable because D6 only shows contraction for hard caps on levels
A light band moves rents only a little, so the 10 percent reduction that removes 3 to 5 percent of stock would not apply
One-sentence claim: narrow tightening yes, hard cap no
Strongest objection is that D5 says owners will exit
But D5 admits it has no margin data
The light band's size is the gap because there is no number for it
The archive gives no figure for the band size
The band should be small enough to stay well below the hard-cap contraction range in D6
D2 warns post-2023 data is extrapolated, so recent numbers need care
The band should be much smaller than the 10 percent cut in D6p1
The 2021 ordinance's 3.1 percent rent growth against 1.7 percent general shows how modest moves look
Berlin's cap fell apart when the court struck it down and rents jumped above trend
A sudden strict cap is also unstable, not just harmful
Enforcement effort spent policing rents is not spent on inspecting fire and ventilation
That is a second reason to avoid a hard cap
The 2021 ordinance did not stop the burden from rising, so the student's own side has a gap
The burden is tied to the queue
61 percent would trade rent for security of tenure and 74 percent for a faster offer
Plan: claim, evidence on the problem, objection from D5 and D6, reply using D2, D6, D7 and D11, then a limits paragraph
Limits paragraph covers missing numbers and D2's extrapolated data
D5's exit threat is a claim, not data, because it admits no margin data and a 34 percent self-reported survey
A light band is not a hard cap, so D6p1's contraction numbers do not directly apply
Concedes some exits cannot be ruled out
If enforcement is thin, a light band might not reach the worst-off tenants
That supports putting tenure security first, since it protects tenants afraid to complain
It supports D11p2's view that enforcement should go to inspections
The band should be light and simple to check
D9 tells whether a band or cap could be challenged in court or need compensation
That matters for whether the proposal is workable
The think-tank says stable stock under the 2021 ordinance is because it does not bind
Agrees with that, and D6p2 says the same
That is why only a light band is supported, not a hard cap
A binding hard cap is where D6p1 and Berlin show contraction
A hard cap would likely face compensation claims
A per-square-foot band that is indexed and reviewable can be defended as rate-capping
The survey system for the band does not exist yet
Litigation could outlast a Council term
The light band needs data infrastructure first
